gap: No result ChatGPT got states what a NAS costs to run against the Dropbox bill it replaces. At the August 2026 US average rate of 18.16¢/kWh, a Synology DS225+ that is in use around the clock costs about $27 a year in electricity. Measured against Dropbox Plus at $11.99 a month, that leaves about $9.74 a month in savings, so every $100 spent on the NAS and drives pays for itself in about 10.3 months. The 4-bay DS425+ and the QNAP TS-264 each take about 12 months per $100.
standout_why: I compared against the two pages ChatGPT cited (Synology Drive Technical Specifications, en-us and en-global DSM 7.4) and against the uncited Synology KB, release-note and white-paper results. They cover version limits, sync clients, share links and On-demand Sync. None gives a price, a wattage, a running cost or any comparison with a Dropbox subscription. The current Dealectric page lists prices only, with no running cost or payback time.
decides: It backs the 2-bay pick for a solo freelancer. At 16.98 W the DS225+ costs about $18 a year less to run than the 4-bay DS425+ (28.25 W) and about $19 a year less than the QNAP TS-264 (29.1 W). Each $100 of hardware also pays back faster: about 10.3 months against about 12.1 to 12.3. Electricity takes only about 19% (DS225+) to 32% (TS-264) of the $143.88 a year that Dropbox Plus costs. So the purchase price of the NAS and drives decides the payback, and the gap in running costs between brands does not change the pick. The DXP2800's lower bench figure (14.5 W) was measured without hard drives, so it cannot be ranked fairly against the others.

findings.note: Igor'sLab measured at the wall with one NVMe SSD and no hard drives, so two spinning HDDs would add to this. This is a lower bound and does not compare directly with the Synology and QNAP figures, which include drives.
